The operational turn toward artificial intelligence infrastructure is reshaping the company's financial profile and cash flow generation. Three key takeaways from management's comments highlight what matters for long-term investors.

According to recent reports, the media division is cutting operating expenses, or recurring costs to run daily operations, by over 20% on a run rate basis. Leadership is moving toward automated platform monetization and partner revenue-sharing models to reach divisional profitability.

Demand for artificial intelligence compute is outpacing data center supply across the market. RUM Group holds an operational edge through its existing 22,000 graphics processing units.

Management is prioritizing capital discipline and pricing discipline as existing contracts expire, focusing on customer prepayments to fund future expansion.

    In the Last Tech Bust, the S&P 500 Lost Money for a Decade. History Says Stocks With the Highest Yields Gained 5.4% a Year.

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (678 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that the AI trade seems to be unwinding fast.
    • In a recent development, however, history offers a useful reference for what held up the last time a technology boom ended.
    • In a recent development, the dot-com bubble burst in March 2000.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Matt DiLallo – Nov 21, 2026 at 5:31PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than S&P 500 Index ›.

    Industry observers note that the AI trade seems to be unwinding fast. The Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC -5.28%) was recently down more than 15% from its early October peak, while the S&P 500 (^GSPC -3.70%) was approaching correction territory, with a roughly 10% slump from its all-time high. Nobody knows how this downturn will play out.

    In a recent development, however, history offers a useful reference for what held up the last time a technology boom ended. From 2000 to 2009, a period that featured the dot-com crash, the S&P 500 posted negative returns, averaging a 0.8% annual decline. High-yielding dividend stocks, on the other hand, delivered an average annual total return of 5.4% over the same period, according to a Wellington Management study published by Hartford Funds. Here's what investors can learn from this history lesson.

    In a recent development, the dot-com bubble burst in March 2000. It led many stock investors to return to fundamentals, focusing on metrics such as a manufacturer's price-to-earnings ratio and dividend yield instead of future monetization potential. Companies that generated real revenue and profits, and returned a portion of their income to investors via dividends, delivered the best returns during this period.

    Sources indicate that wellington sorted dividend-paying stocks into five groups by yield, from the top 20% of payers to the bottom 20%. In the 2000s, the highest-yielding group gained 5.4% a year, while the lowest-yielding payers lost 1.7% a year. To put this in dollars, $1,000 compounding at 5.4% for 10 years grows to about $1,690, while $1,000 shrinking at 0.8% per year ends up near $923.

    The decade before the dot-com bust looked very different for high-yielding dividend stocks. In the 1990s, the lowest-yielding payers kept pace with the S&P 500, while the highest-yielding group trailed it by a meaningful amount. Meanwhile, the last six years look a lot like the late 1990s. Since 2020, the lowest-yielding payers have beaten the market, while the highest-yielding group has trailed.

    The highest-yielding dividend stocks have outperformed the market in five of 10 time periods from 1930 to 2025. That's the same percentage as the lowest yielders. The best performers were companies with higher dividend yields, though not the highest. These companies prioritized dividend payments (and growth) without sacrificing financial flexibility. This cohort outperformed the S&P 500 in six of those 10 periods, including in the 2000s (4.4% annualized return). They also delivered solid performance leading up to the dot-com crash (15.6% returns in the 1990s).

    Here are three practical tips investors can employ in their own portfolios based on the data on dividend stocks:.

    A high yield can be as much a warning as a reward. A stock's yield rises when its price falls, and sometimes the market is pricing in a dividend cut. The data on cutters show how costly that can be. From 1973 through 2025, S&P 500 companies that cut or eliminated their dividends returned an average of -1% a year, compared with 10.2% for companies that raised theirs and 7.7% for the average stock, according to Ned Davis Research data published by Hartford. Cutters were also the most volatile group.

    Sources indicate that the last time a technology boom ended, the stocks that paid the most were the ones that held up best, while the lowest-yielding payers lost more than the market. That doesn't mean history will repeat itself, and the biggest yields carry their own risks, as dividend cutters show. However, the data makes a case for adding some yield to your portfolio before the next cycle turns.

    10 stocks we like better than iQIYI ›.

    On its third quarter of 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 16, 2026, iQiyi (IQ -10.96%) declared that content costs declined as it returned to non-GAAP (adjusted accounting) operating profit. The streaming platform is shifting toward artificial intelligence production and decentralized content sharing to lower upfront financial risk. Three takeaways from the call highlight this strategic pivot.

    Shifting content creation toward revenue sharing allows third-party creators to absorb production costs while iQiyi pays based on viewer performance. This model lowers fixed cash outlays and reduces the platform's dependence on unpredictable blockbuster releases.

    Deploying AIGC (artificial intelligence-generated content) helps the platform turn existing IP (intellectual property) into commercial projects much faster. The three chapters of The Ferry Man series each recouped their entire budget during their first week online.

    Short-form dramas--episodes running 15 to 30 minutes--offer quick production turns and lower risk than traditional serialized demonstrates. iQiyi captured the top market share in this fast-growing category during the quarter.

    Content costs are falling while the platform builds dedicated online creator tools and expands connected television advertising. Management is strengthening its subscription service and creator network while using artificial intelligence to accelerate output.

    By focusing on disciplined investments and expanding revenue-sharing models, management aims to turn efficiency gains into consistent long-term cash flow.

    Robinhood shares fall as crypto slump weighs on profits, offsetting gains in latest businesses

    📅 27 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (341 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Robinhood shares were down around 8% in pre-market trading on Wednesday as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earnings despite growth in options trading and prediction markets.
    • Here's how the brokerage performed in its quarter ended Sept.
    • It has been revealed that robinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Robinhood shares were down around 8% in pre-market trading on Wednesday as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earnings despite growth in options trading and prediction markets.

    Here's how the brokerage performed in its quarter ended Sept. 30, compared with Wall Street estimates, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:.

    It has been revealed that robinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago. Revenue represented a 12% increase from $1.27 billion in the same quarter last year.

    Despite that gain, transaction-based revenue of $867 million came in below Wall Street estimates from StreetAccount of $879 million, putting focus on whether Robinhood can sustain momentum across its trading businesses and reduce its reliance on volatile market activity.

    Sources indicate that robinhood has been diversifying its business as it tries to expand its brokerage app into a broader financial services platform. Options trading and event contracts have become increasingly vital sources of transaction revenue, while the organization has continued to invest in wealth management, subscriptions and other offerings.

    Transaction-based revenue grew 19% from the same period last year to $867 million, driven primarily by a more than 500% increase in event contracts revenue. Additionally, options revenue grew 31% to $399 million and equities revenue rose 41% to $121 million.

    Those gains were partially offset by cryptocurrency revenue, which fell 55% to $120 million.

    Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma told CNBC event contracts on crypto movements did well in the quarter, offering investors another way to express a view on crypto despite the slump in prices and spot trading.

    It has been revealed that net deposits on the Robinhood platform totaled $15.7 billion for the quarter, equal to a 17% annualized growth rate based on total platform assets at the end of Q2 2026. Over the past year, net deposits totaled $71 billion, representing 21% growth compared with total platform assets at the end of Q3 2025.

    —With reporting from CNBC's Robert Hum and Kate Rooney.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The ongoing earnings season, Middle East tensions and buzz ahead of the U.S.
    • Investors looking beyond the short-term noise and focusing on long-term returns can track top Wall Street analysts to pick the right stocks, backed by strong research.
    • Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The ongoing earnings season, Middle East tensions and buzz ahead of the U.S. midterm elections have been keeping investors busy. Further, worries about elevated artificial intelligence spending are weighing on investor sentiment.

    Investors looking beyond the short-term noise and focusing on long-term returns can track top Wall Street analysts to pick the right stocks, backed by strong research.

    Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

    According to recent reports, this week's first stock pick is Datadog, an AI-powered observability and security platform. The firm will announce its results for the third quarter on Nov. 4. Datadog is seeing strong demand for its offerings, thanks to cloud migration and rapid AI adoption. TipRanks' KPIs tool for DDOG shows the growth in its customer base over the past few years amid increasing market penetration and growing adoption of its products.

    According to recent reports, heading into Q3 FY26 earnings, Bank of America analyst Koji Ikeda reiterated a buy rating on Datadog stock and raised his price target to $335 from $305. The analyst noted that industry checks and data indicate that infrastructure software demand is strengthening, with AI increasingly driving usage and growth.

    Recent findings suggest that ikeda called Datadog and Atlassian his top picks, saying that companies that can show that AI is a tailwind to growth could see their valuation rerate, even at premium multiples. He added that the total addressable market for observability is growing faster than anticipated, driven by accelerated growth of enterprise AI and the rapid ramp of consumer AI agents.

    In a recent development, the five-star analyst believes that focus will be on revenue growth, which he estimates to be 28.7% for Q3 FY26 versus the Street's consensus of 29.1%. Ikeda thinks that the market is underestimating the growth prospects of DDOG's security products. Meanwhile, he cautioned investors about concentration risk related to large customers.

    "We think results will be supportive of our long-term thesis that Datadog is a strong share gainer in the rapidly expanding observability opportunity," remarked Ikeda.

    Ikeda ranks No. 673 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 55% of the time, delivering an average return of 10.9%. See Datadog Statistics on TipRanks.

    Sources indicate that the next pick, semiconductor giant Nvidia, is also benefiting from AI-driven demand for its products. After attending Nvidia's GTC Berlin conference, Morgan Stanley analyst Joseph Moore reaffirmed a buy rating on NVDA stock with a price target of $300, calling it a top pick in the semiconductor space.

    Sources indicate that the five-star analyst said that the conference supported his thesis that Nvidia continues to effectively navigate bottlenecks in the supply chain, land/power/shell, and funding. In fact, Moore is "convinced that all 3 aspects are opportunities for NVDA.".

    Sources indicate that while Nvidia's GTC Berlin offered no major updates, Moore noted the conference reflected that the manufacturer continues to add to its significant advantages heading into 2027. The analyst said that Vera Rubin is gaining momentum, though details on next year's Rubin Ultra were lighter than expected.

    In a recent development, with demand outpacing supply, Moore noted that focus is on closing the gap. In this regard, he highlighted the supply chain deals on substrate, packaging and testing. While the analyst continues to view TSMC 3 nm wafer supply as the biggest challenge, he expects it to ease over time.

    Moore ranks No. 142 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 59% of the time, delivering an average return of 23.4%. See Nvidia Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

    Aerospace firm SpaceX recently declared solid third-quarter results, with its AI revenue surging to $7.56 billion from $813 million in the prior-year quarter.

    Impressed by the results, Needham analyst Ryan Koontz reiterated a buy rating on SPCX stock with a price target of $250. Koontz highlighted that SpaceX's Q3 results significantly exceeded expectations, proving that the company's vertically integrated business model is driving massive scale.

    Furthermore, Koontz emphasized the 195.2% sequential growth in SpaceX's AI revenue, fueled by wholesale spot compute deals. He noted management's increasing focus on its AI strategy, given that it is optimistic about adding 10 gigawatts of incremental capacity during 2027.

    "With increasing confidence on Starship re-use, we meaningfully increase our estimates," noted Koontz.

    Sources indicate that koontz ranks No. 357 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 42% of the time, delivering an average return of 23.7%. See SpaceX Technical Analysis on TipRanks.

    Top Wall Street analysts like these 3 dividend stocks for consistent income

    📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (898 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Democrats' midterm election win has put the artificial intelligence trade in question, as voters clearly expressed opposition to the rapid buildout of data centers.
    • In this scenario, investors can add dividend-paying stocks to their portfolios to earn steady income.
    • Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Democrats' midterm election win has put the artificial intelligence trade in question, as voters clearly expressed opposition to the rapid buildout of data centers. The stock market could remain volatile amid AI trade concerns, macro uncertainties, and geopolitical tensions.

    In this scenario, investors can add dividend-paying stocks to their portfolios to earn steady income. However, the extensive universe of dividend stocks can make selection challenging. Top Wall Street analysts' recommendations can help investors shortlist attractive dividend stocks, as these experts assign ratings after in-depth financial analysis.

    Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

    Viper Energy (VNOM) is a subsidiary of Diamondback and owns and acquires mineral and royalty interests, primarily in the Permian Basin. The company reported upbeat third-quarter earnings, supported by recent acquisitions and continued development activity from Diamondback and third-party operators. Viper announced a base cash dividend of 50 cents per share for Q3 2026, payable on Nov. 19. Based on the base and variable dividends announced over the past 12 months, VNOM's dividend yield stands at 5.7%.

    Following the Q3 results, TD Cowen analyst Aaron Bilkoski reiterated a buy rating on Viper Energy stock with a price target of $61. The analyst noted that the firm delivered solid Q3 results, with production, including oil and natural gas liquids, exceeding both TD Cowen and consensus estimates.

    The 5-star analyst highlighted that the key revision was the announcement of two royalty acquisitions for $809 million in cash, including deferred consideration, and $82 million of newly issued shares.

    Industry observers note that given the recently announced base dividend hike, Bilkoski expects Viper to direct incremental free cash flow toward buybacks. While the acquisitions increase leverage, the analyst believes that Viper has enough capacity for opportunistic buybacks.

    Sources indicate that bilkoski noted that Viper has historically delivered one of the highest production per share growth profiles in his royalty coverage, but still trades at a notable discount to the royalty peer average and the company's historical FCF yield range. "In our view, its above-average growth warrants a higher valuation," said the analyst.

    Recent findings suggest that bilkoski ranks No. 525 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 12.80%. See Viper Energy Stock Buybacks on TipRanks.

    In a recent development, exxon Mobil (XOM) reported robust Q3 2026 profits, as its U.S. refineries boosted production to capitalize on the high diesel fuel prices sparked by the conflict in the Middle East. The oil and gas giant announced a quarterly dividend of $1.07 per share, payable on Dec. 10, reflecting a 3.9% increase. This marks Exxon's 44th consecutive year of dividend increases. At an annualized dividend of $4.28 per share, XOM offers a yield of 2.53%.

    Impressed by the Q3 print, TD Cowen analyst Jason Gabelman reiterated a buy rating on Exxon stock and raised his price target to $193 from $180 to reflect higher downstream earnings, with the expectation of increased mid-cycle margins.

    Recent findings suggest that gabelman noted that the strength in Exxon's refining business continues to offset Middle East-related headwinds. He added that the organization increased its ownership in LNG projects, which should reduce its Middle East concentration over time from 75% to 50% and lower the likelihood of diversification-focused mergers and acquisitions. Beyond LNG, Gabelman expects Exxon's growth in the 2030s to come from Guyana, Kashagan, Permian, and possibly Venezuela.

    Gabelman noted that Exxon announced a dividend hike of nearly 4% and plans to maintain buybacks at $20 billion for 2027. "The decision to maintain reduces the pro-cyclicality nature of the buyback," said the analyst.

    Gabelman ranks No. 347 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 66% of the time, delivering an average return of 16.90%. See Exxon Mobil Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

    Sources indicate that williams (WMB), which owns and operates energy infrastructure to deliver natural gas, reported strong third-quarter results. The company unveiled a quarterly dividend of $0.525 per share, or $2.10 per share annualized, payable on Dec. 28. WMB offers a dividend yield of 3.09%.

    In reaction to the Q3 2026 results, CIBC analyst Robert Catellier reaffirmed a buy rating on Williams stock with a price target of $82. The analyst noted that Q3 results were essentially in line with expectations and reflected continued strength in execution across WMB's infrastructure portfolio.

    Catellier said that Williams' Q3 performance was driven by higher transmission, storage, and power generation revenues, as well as contributions from the Momentum Midstream acquisition.

    Industry observers note that he noted that Williams maintained its full-year EBITDA guidance of $8.3 billion to $8.5 billion. In fact, results are tracking toward the higher end of the guidance range, backed by contributions from recently completed projects and the Momentum Midstream deal. WMB continues to target long-term EBITDA compound annual growth rate of at least 11% through 2030.

    Catellier expects WMB's long-term targets to be supported by incremental transmission and storage opportunities, including Transco's Southeast Supply Enhancement II project and an 84 MMcf/d expansion of the Garden Connector project.

    Catellier ranks No. 667 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 66% of the time, delivering an average return of 9.60%. See Williams Technical Analysis on TipRanks.

    #73705. Anthropic raises $93.5 billion total as underwriters scoop up ‘greenshoe’ overallotment

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (417 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    Anthropic raises $93.5 billion total as underwriters scoop up ‘greenshoe’ overallotment

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (417 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Anthropic underwriters have officially exercised their overallotment of shares in the historic initial public offering, bringing the total raised to $93.5 billion, according to a release Friday.
    • The artificial intelligence tech giant raised $81.3 billion on Wednesday and netted an additional $12.2 billion through the overallotment, surpassing SpaceX, which held a record IPO in June.
    • Anthropic stated it sold an aggregate of 1,127,000,000 shares of its Class A common stock at $83 per share in the offering.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Anthropic underwriters have officially exercised their overallotment of shares in the historic initial public offering, bringing the total raised to $93.5 billion, according to a release Friday.

    The artificial intelligence tech giant raised $81.3 billion on Wednesday and netted an additional $12.2 billion through the overallotment, surpassing SpaceX, which held a record IPO in June.

    Anthropic stated it sold an aggregate of 1,127,000,000 shares of its Class A common stock at $83 per share in the offering. It sold 980 million shares on Wednesday and its underwriters had the option to purchase up to an additional 147 million shares by Friday as part of the overallotment, which is commonly referred to as the "greenshoe.".

    Shares of the Claude maker opened trading at $111.50 on the Nasdaq on Thursday, but slid throughout the day and closed at $97.17. The stock sank 12% in premarket trading on Friday during a broad tech sell-off.

    Sources indicate that in addition to the sale of its Class A common stock, Anthropic closed a concurrent sale of its Class N common stock after a group of tech companies, including Advanced Micro Devices, Google, Microsoft, Nvidia and others, agreed to participate in a $26 billion private placement at the IPO price. Anthropic said Friday that aggregate gross proceeds from its IPO, including the private placement, totaled $119.5 billion, before deducting offering expenses.

    Anthropic dodged an unforgiving series of obstacles on its road to the Nasdaq on Thursday, as investors brooded over Jensen Huang's shocking ouster at Nvidia, voters' stinging rebuke of the tech during the midterms and whether rising interest rates would stymie industry prepares for a multitrillion-dollar AI infrastructure buildout.

    Industry observers note that CEO Dario Amodei co-founded the company in 2021 after he and a handful of other researchers, including his sister Daniela, quit their jobs at OpenAI, now Anthropic's chief rival. Anthropic is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude, which have captivated the corporate world and fueled the company's historic rise.

    The siblings celebrated the IPO as a "milestone" in an interview with CNBC on Thursday, but mentioned there's more work ahead for Anthropic.

    Recent findings suggest that "For us, it's like one stop on the journey," Daniela Amodei said. "We think about this as, 'Wow, this is an incredible moment for Anthropic for our mission, but we're going to wake up tomorrow and we're going to be the same tech giant.'".

    #73703. Breaking: Trump states he discussed Jensen Huang with Xi; Bessent tells CNBC Nvidia chip export policy is unchanged

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (891 w)
    📖 Baca
    Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Trump states he discussed Jensen Huang with Xi; Bessent tells CNBC Nvidia chip export policy is unchanged

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (891 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that president Donald Trump on Friday said he and Chinese leader Xi Jinping discussed their shared affinity for former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during their talks in China this week.
    • Industry observers note that "I did discuss that with President Xi, and he stated, 'Oh, brilliant, brilliant!
    • Asked earlier Friday on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" if Huang, a close ally of Trump's, had come up in "any of your discussions with the Chinese," Bessent noted "no," without elaborating.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that president Donald Trump on Friday said he and Chinese leader Xi Jinping discussed their shared affinity for former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during their talks in China this week. Earlier in the day, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the ousted leader was not mentioned in separate talks he had with Chinese officials.

    Industry observers note that "I did discuss that with President Xi, and he stated, 'Oh, brilliant, brilliant! He's a brilliant man.' He is," Trump said at a White House press conference.

    Asked earlier Friday on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" if Huang, a close ally of Trump's, had come up in "any of your discussions with the Chinese," Bessent noted "no," without elaborating.

    A senior Trump administration official later said that both Trump's and Bessent's remarks were correct, and that both were addressing their own conversations. The official spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss those conversations.

    Trump also reiterated that he would like to see Huang — who was replaced by interim CEO Colette Kress after resigning amid allegations of an extramarital affair with a Chinese spy — be restored as Nvidia's CEO.

    Industry observers note that "I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance," Trump said. "You know, we're a country of second chances, and I'd love to be able to see him. That's a very important firm to us, and he put us in a position where we are literally 10 years advanced over other companies.".

    Nvidia's board is not considering bringing Huang back, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC earlier this week.

    Sources indicate that the president's comments came amid growing scrutiny of advanced U.S. chips, including those made by Nvidia, ending up in China either legally or by being diverted via third countries.

    Both Trump's and Bessent's remarks are potentially an indication that the Trump administration may not focus on cracking down on China's efforts to acquire advanced chips.

    It has been revealed that bessent suggested that U.S. policy allowing the sale of Nvidia's powerful H200 AI chips to China remains unchanged following the talks in Shenzhen this week.

    It has been revealed that "We've already agreed that the ... H200s are the threshold level of chips that could be sold to the Chinese, and, you know, that continues as planned," Bessent mentioned.

    "I wouldn't anticipate any change in the policy," he added after CNBC's Sara Eisen noted that Nvidia stated it had stopped selling H200s to China.

    Industry observers note that the administration ignoring the subject of Huang's affair with a possible Chinese spy — whose Singapore-based company Megaspeed has been accused of acting as a cutout for Beijing — contrasts with the importance Trump has placed on beating China in the race to artificial intelligence dominance. It could suggest that despite his support for the U.S. AI industry, Trump is less concerned with addressing China's ongoing efforts to acquire U.S. semiconductors.

    Sources indicate that trump has also defended Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who has come under fire from multiple directions for reportedly slow-walking export restrictions on Chinese chip sales. "I understand both sides of it," Trump said on Monday when he also said he's like to see Huang back as CEO.

    Bessent's appearance on CNBC came after Trump's return from a tour through Asia that saw him meet with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China.

    The meeting was historic as the first time the leaders of the three countries had met without other nations' counterparts. But the trilateral summit appeared to yield few deliverables on any number of the most pressing global issues related to the countries, including the Ukraine and Iran wars or the ongoing AI race.

    Bessent told CNBC on Friday that there was a "robust discussion" between Trump and Xi on trade policy and AI.

    They "agreed that humans should always be involved in any military decisions that SI makes, and the SI should not be allowed to be autonomous for major military actions," he said, abbreviating the term "super intelligence," Trump's attempted rebrand of AI.

    In a CNBC appearance last week, Bessent lamented the "leakage" of U.S.-made AI chips to China and blamed the Commerce Department, led by Lutnick, for slow-walking export controls on suspected Chinese cutouts like Megaspeed.

    Multiple Trump administration leaders have long sought to impose export restrictions on Megaspeed, but Commerce "has the pen" and "you will have to ask them about their internal processes," Bessent noted in that interview.

    On Friday, however, Bessent was much more tight-lipped.

    In a recent development, asked if there is a dispute between him and Lutnick over how aggressively the U.S. should be pursuing Chinese export controls, Bessent stated, "I think we're all committed to following President Trump's instructions.".

    Recent findings suggest that "I think we are going to see that the ... proper chip restrictions are in place, and the remote access has been curtailed," he added. Commerce recently took steps to close one of China's paths to accessing AI processors.

    Correction: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent spoke to CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." A previous version of this story misstated the name of the show.

    Editor's note: This story and headline have been updated following additional information provided by the Trump administration about the nature of Bessent's and Trump's meetings in China.

    Latest Update: Tokenization platform Securitize gains 10% postmarket on Q3 results, move into asset-backed finance

    📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (442 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Tokenization platform Securitize climbed about 10% postmarket after reporting third quarter growth alongside increased operating expenses, and announcing an expansion into asset-backed finance through a strategic acquisition.
    • Recent findings suggest that miami-based Securitize, which made its public market debut in July, operates in the relatively fresh corner of the crypto equity universe involved in institutional tokenization infrastructure.
    • The growth came as bullish sentiment around tokenization gained traction throughout the third quarter, ahead of the Security and Exchange Commission formalizing the long awaited Innovation Exemption on Sept.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Tokenization platform Securitize climbed about 10% postmarket after reporting third quarter growth alongside increased operating expenses, and announcing an expansion into asset-backed finance through a strategic acquisition.

    Recent findings suggest that miami-based Securitize, which made its public market debut in July, operates in the relatively fresh corner of the crypto equity universe involved in institutional tokenization infrastructure. Tokenized assets on the platform grew 9% in the third quarter, to $4.8 billion, from the same period a year ago. Aggregate transaction volume rose 20% from a year ago, to $4.3 billion. Revenue of $11.5 million was up 28% from last year.

    The growth came as bullish sentiment around tokenization gained traction throughout the third quarter, ahead of the Security and Exchange Commission formalizing the long awaited Innovation Exemption on Sept. 17, which created a temporary pathway for trading of certain tokenized stocks and strengthened the regulatory outlook.

    Profitability is still meaningfully below year-ago levels, due in part to costs associated with going public over the summer, as well as the scaling up of the tokenization business at an active time for the entire sector, Securitize CEO Carlos Domingo told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

    Securitize reinforced "certain areas of the company like finance, compliance, legal [and] cybersecurity," which increased corporate costs "compared to a year ago when we were privately held," Domingo said. "We're in in a very good position. The adjusted EBITDA … is improving significantly from previous quarters.".

    Securitize reported an adjusted EBITDA loss of $2 million, compared with positive adjusted EBITDA of $3.6 million a year ago, better than a $5.5 million loss in the second quarter. The tech giant posted a 183% increase in operating costs and expenses.

    Industry observers note that also on Monday, the Securitize board authorized a $50 million share buyback and announced the acquisition of River One, an institutional asset-backed financing platform developing technology to connect stablecoin capital with traditional lending markets. Terms were not disclosed.

    Securitize sees an opportunity to modernize the $9 trillion market for asset backed finance by using stablecoins to finance real world assets, generate yield and tokenize investment positions and credit products, Domingo said.The acquisition also marks an expansion beyond Securitize's core niche markets at a time when tokenization's competitive landscape is growing, with traditional asset managers like BlackRock and Franklin Templeton, and established financial market infrastructure providers like DTCC and Broadridge, entering the industry.

    "We have been very active in tokenized funds, treasuries [and] yield … And we've been obviously recently very active in tokenized stocks, so this adds another piece of the puzzle in the emerging tokenization space for us to capture revenue growth.".

    #73695. Warsh wants Fed officials to talk less. Instead, they’re talking more

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1060 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    Warsh wants Fed officials to talk less. Instead, they’re talking more

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1060 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, in his first six months as Federal Reserve chairman, Kevin Warsh has diligently avoided signaling where he sees monetary policy and interest rates headed.
    • Fed officials have been rushing to the microphones lately, voicing sometimes conflicting opinions on how the central bank should be handling an inflation bug that the economy can't seem to shake.
    • Most agree that rates should be raised — and soon.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, in his first six months as Federal Reserve chairman, Kevin Warsh has diligently avoided signaling where he sees monetary policy and interest rates headed. His colleagues have been only too happy to fill the void.

    Fed officials have been rushing to the microphones lately, voicing sometimes conflicting opinions on how the central bank should be handling an inflation bug that the economy can't seem to shake.

    Most agree that rates should be raised — and soon. Some are willing to hike at a measured pace as conditions play out, while others, such as Governor Christopher Waller and St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem, entertain the thought of more aggressive hikes in a shorter period of time.

    In a recent development, largely on the sidelines in the debate is Warsh, who has expressed disdain for that sort of forward guidance and argued that it handcuffs policymakers long before they actually have to make a decision. But that hasn't stopped most of the other 18 officials who sit in on Federal Open Market Committee meetings.

    In fact, according to a Bank of America analysis, there has been more so-called Fedspeak in the past two weeks than in any similar period since the start of 2025.

    "Warsh's refusal to guide markets might be encouraging the rest of the FOMC to speak more, not less," Bank of America economist Aditya Bhave stated in a note Thursday.

    "There is always a range of views across the 19 FOMC participants. Typically, the Chair would weigh in, indicating to markets whether the hawks or doves are in ascendence," he added. "Absent this leadership, however, both sides might feel incentivized to speak more often and more forcefully.".

    The increasingly vocal debate comes at a critical time for the Fed and has myriad policy implications.

    Bhave noted "a deepening divide" on the FOMC. The Fed's decision not to increase its benchmark rate at its October meeting "increasingly looks like a mistake," and as a result "the hawks have been very vocal of late," he wrote. Leading the charge is Waller, who has raised the possibility of hiking by half a percentage point when the committee next meets in December.

    Minutes from the October meeting hint at the tension, particularly when it comes to Warsh's refusal to provide guidance.

    The summary related that some officials who were looking for a hike in October "could have supported no change in the federal funds rate provided that it was clearly understood by market participants that further tightening was likely" — a statement that points toward the forward guidance that Warsh has insisted the Fed avoid.

    According to recent reports, the minutes "revealed that some officials favoring a hike would have accepted a hold if the Fed had clearly communicated further tightening," market veteran Ed Yardeni wrote Thursday. "Warsh's communication philosophy may thus be limiting the Fed's flexibility precisely when it needs it most.".

    Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, who voted against the October pause in favor of a quarter-point hike, tiptoed around the forward guidance glitch during a recent public appearance.

    Sources indicate that prefacing some observations she made about where she sees policy headed, Hammack noted that, "Those are not promises. Those are not commitments. They're not forward guidance, which is a hot-button topic. But what they are are a conditional set of expectations of where I think the economy can go, based on what I'm seeing.".

    Hammack's comments illustrate a needle that Fed officials have been trying to thread: continuing to be transparent about their thinking without appearing locked into a future policy that changing economic conditions could render obsolete.

    Speaking Thursday, Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee framed the argument around credibility.

    "I am sympathetic to the view that [Warsh] has expressed that let's not be so, in in our language, forward guidance-oriented, saying here is what I think rates are going to be at the next meeting," Goolsbee noted, calling such pronouncements "falsely precise.".

    However, he rapidly separated forward guidance from transparency.

    Recent findings suggest that "I think central banks should be careful about doing anything that undermines credibility," Goolsbee said. "That said, I also think that it's pretty important [that] each person who sits around that table explain how they see the world. What do you see in business conditions? You don't want to surprise everybody.".

    Taking a slightly different tack, Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson, in a speech Thursday on policy communication, insisted that markets can figure out where policymakers are going without specific guidance so long as they understand how economic developments will influence decisions.

    Paulson also defended the variety of voices coming from the Fed.

    "But volume is not the same as clarity," she said. "The measure is not how much we say. It is whether we are understood." The mixture of voices "guards against any single communication becoming the only one that matters.".

    Financial markets have taken the plethora of Fed communications and interpreted it in a fairly hawkish way.

    Traders are implying a 100% chance of at least a quarter percentage point hike in December, with a very small probability of a half-point move, according to the CME Group's FedWatch. From there, odds are high for a follow-up increase in January, then perhaps one more before the end of 2027.

    While current inflation indicators are running above 3%, compared to the Fed's 2% target, market measures of longer-term inflation have declined.

    It has been revealed that five-year forward expectations, as indicated through the Treasury market, are at their lowest since April. That suggests investors could be less concerned about inflation over the longer term, even as policymakers warn that current price pressures remain elevated.

    Still, a sclerotic communications strategy from the Fed amid volatile economic and geopolitical currents could prove dangerous ahead.

    "The result of this back-and-forth is undue rates volatility in already turbulent times," BofA's Bhave said.

    For his part, Warsh has been advocating for a "family fight" atmosphere inside the Fed, arguing that competing viewpoints deserve a full airing as the committee works towards decisions.

    In a recent development, "There are benefits to shaping the market's future expectations. Perhaps this is part of the 'family fight' that Warsh keeps referencing in his pressers," mentioned Tom Graff, chief investment officer at advisory firm Facet. "That family fight seems to be happening out in public.".

    #73692. Data center construction costs soar 13% in 2026

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (524 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    Data center construction costs soar 13% in 2026

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (524 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, the demand for large-scale data centers in the U.S.
    • Industry observers note that all that resulted in costs rising 13% year-over-year to more than twice the global rate, according to a latest report from Turner & Townsend, a global project management firm.
    • In a recent development, the report looked at over 500 live or recently completed projects in 62 global markets.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, the demand for large-scale data centers in the U.S. this year, driven by the need for computing power for artificial intelligence, grew well beyond the supply of powered land and the labor to build these structures. It also pushed timelines and risk for contractors.

    Industry observers note that all that resulted in costs rising 13% year-over-year to more than twice the global rate, according to a latest report from Turner & Townsend, a global project management firm. The gain this year was about three times the last ten-year average.

    In a recent development, the report looked at over 500 live or recently completed projects in 62 global markets. It also included a survey of 400 experts in the global data center industry.

    While there was some stabilization in cost inflation this year, it was not enough to offset the huge growth in not just demand but speed of construction and delivery.

    In a recent development, "More aggressive schedules tie to contractors in particular and subcontractors baking in more risk allowances in their pricing," said Paul Barry, North America data center lead for Turner & Townsend. "So whether that's acceleration allowances, whether that's more overtime and labor attraction allowances, even just higher fees for taking on the risk of delivering at a faster pace than what they would traditionally take on.".

    All of those things, combined with the spike in demand and the strain on the supply chain, translate into higher costs, he added.

    In a recent development, capital expenditure on global data centers is projected to rise from about $800 billion this year to $1.8 trillion per year in 2050, according to a recent report from PwC. The U.S. is expected to capture almost half of all global investment in AI infrastructure, which includes both data centers and chips.

    Sources indicate that power is, of course, key to all data centers, and 56% of those surveyed by Turner & Townsend globally said it was a major obstacle to delivery. Just over half said utility connections typically take between one and two years, and almost a third reported timeframes of over two years. Costs for power vary regionally — from $15.01 per watt in Silicon Valley to $10.51 per watt in Dallas, based on a typical 60-megawatt design.As with every type of construction in the U.S., labor continues to be a significant headwind. Just over one quarter of respondents said their contractor capacity, that is, the ability to manage construction backlogs, was sufficient.

    Going forward, Barry remarked he expects costs to moderate somewhat, with cost increases in the 6% to 10% range in the next year. A lot of the major projects have already started or are starting now, so cost risk has been baked into those contracts.

    "If this demand continues, then there'll be more continued flow of project starts and so on, but I think we've hit a substantial surge in 2026, especially of new big major projects that have been procured," said Barry.

    CNBC's Property Play with Diana Olick covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, delivered weekly to your inbox.

    Trump vows to stop U.S. companies from building data centers abroad, threatens 'tremendous tax'

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (375 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • President Donald Trump on Friday stated U.S.
    • "We're going to fight very hard for the data centers," Trump said at a White House press conference before announcing the new policy — which apparently came as news to his own staff.
    • Industry observers note that "I don't know if that's a breaking story," Trump said.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    President Donald Trump on Friday stated U.S. companies will be banned from building data centers in other countries and will face a "tremendous tax" penalty if they do so.

    "We're going to fight very hard for the data centers," Trump said at a White House press conference before announcing the new policy — which apparently came as news to his own staff.

    Industry observers note that "I don't know if that's a breaking story," Trump said. "I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now they're here.".

    Trump's latest push for more data-center construction in the U.S. came despite Americans repeatedly stating — and showing with their votes — that they dislike the structures.

    CNBC's All-America Economic Survey found that 64% of registered voters opposed an AI data center within 10 miles of their home, while just 13% of respondents said they would support one.

    If Trump follows through on his threat to clamp down on overseas data center construction, he will have to contend with the fact that numerous U.S. tech giants — including Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta and Oracle — have already built them in other countries.

    International expansion represents a growth opportunity for the top cloud infrastructure providers, which want to serve clients from data centers that are nearby, sometimes to meet regulatory requirements.

    Trump stated Friday, however, that if companies want to continue building the centers outside the U.S., "they can, but we're going to put a tremendous tax on them.".

    Industry observers note that "We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy, and they have everything. They're tremendous assets," Trump remarked.

    Representatives at cloud providers Amazon, Google, Microsoft and Oracle did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

    Trump's remarks came a day after Trump met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in China for a trilateral summit that appeared to produce few concrete deliverables on an array of pressing global problems.

    Xi "congratulated me on how well we're doing" in artificial intelligence, Trump mentioned, using his preferred term "super intelligence," which he said the Chinese president also likes better.

    — CNBC's Jordan Novet and Annie Palmer contributed reporting.

    #73679. Latest Update: AI is changing software engineering — and some developers miss the struggle

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (967 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: AI is changing software engineering — and some developers miss the struggle

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (967 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When Gemma Rodgers began her computer science degree in 2002, software engineering was seen as a future-proof and lucrative career.
    • Industry observers note that it's an industry that has always moved fast, Rodgers, a software developer based in the U.K., told CNBC.
    • As AI coding tools help engineers write, debug and test code faster than ever, some are mourning the job they used to have.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When Gemma Rodgers began her computer science degree in 2002, software engineering was seen as a future-proof and lucrative career. It appealed to people who enjoyed getting into the weeds of code, tracking down bugs and building programs from scratch.

    Industry observers note that it's an industry that has always moved fast, Rodgers, a software developer based in the U.K., told CNBC. But the arrival of artificial intelligence has accelerated the pace, with AI tools now part of the daily work of every software engineer she knows. In a 2026 Stack Overflow survey, 83% of software developer respondents remarked they use at least one AI tool.

    As AI coding tools help engineers write, debug and test code faster than ever, some are mourning the job they used to have. Rodgers has always loved the sense of accomplishment that comes from piecing together different parts of code to find a solution, particularly when she's spent days, or even weeks, trying to fix a stubborn bug.

    "The sense of joy and fun that I used to experience by having a challenge and then having to work that out, it's been removed somewhat," she said. "Now you can sometimes do it in a few prompts, and it's great — but it's a breadcrumb of joy, not a full meal of joy.".

    Recent findings suggest that rodgers is not alone in feeling nostalgic about the not-so-old days. Software engineers have taken to social media to describe missing their old way of working, when they could get into a flow state with code for hours at a time.

    Sources indicate that still, AI tools can be useful and have lowered the barrier to entry significantly. "It's becoming an industry where a lot of people have been able to thrive who wouldn't necessarily have been able to thrive 10 years ago, five years ago, even three years ago," Rodgers stated.

    It's also vital that the core skills engineers have traditionally learned on the job are not lost, she said. AI tools and internet services can go down unexpectedly, and engineers still need to know how to investigate problems and work through solutions themselves.

    "The sorts of skills that we were taught years ago are kind of being lost because [engineers are] having to just churn work out," Rodgers added.

    Industry observers note that the job itself is changing, too. James Broadhead, chief technology officer of AI decision-making manufacturer Taktile, told CNBC that engineers who might previously have spent three weeks building a prototype can now generate 10 in an afternoon. The hardest part of that, he said, is "having the judgment to decide which of those are any good.".

    "The [AI] agents are spitting out so much code that [engineers] haven't read it all anymore," Broadhead mentioned. "It used to be you'd build up a sense of comfort and awareness of how the whole code base was structured, but now the whole thing changes all the time.".

    Joshua Wöhle, CEO of London-based AI training organization Mindstone, told CNBC he sees a growing divide between workers who know how to use AI effectively and those who don't.

    The industry used to talk about "10X engineers," he remarked, who were dramatically more productive than their peers. Now, AI is widening that gap even further to produce "100X engineers.".

    Industry observers note that wöhle believes companies will increasingly have to decide whether to help employees catch up with AI or prioritize those who can get the most out of it. But he also understands why some engineers might struggle to adapt.

    The people who once excelled at the job were often those who loved writing and working through code, he said, and those are not necessarily the current top performers.

    Industry observers note that "That's the grief that is very, very real," Wöhle noted. "The thing you love doing is no longer the thing the firm should be paying for, to a degree, because it's no longer adding the value to the company that it used to.".

    But not every engineer sees the move away from hands-on coding as a bad thing. Chris Sees, a software engineer of more than 20 years and CEO of London-based virtual office firm Hoxton Mix, told CNBC that AI gives developers more time to tackle interesting problems. He views AI as a capable junior engineer that still needs supervision.

    Industry observers note that "The important thing is knowing what to delegate and when human judgement is needed," Sees remarked. "We'd be silly to think AI gets everything right, and I know I get a lot of satisfaction out of proving and spotting where it has gone wrong.".

    In a recent development, even so, Sees worries about what happens to the next generation of engineers if AI takes over the routine coding and debugging through which they traditionally learned. Those tasks are "where you learn lessons and build scar tissue," he mentioned, and companies need to make sure AI becomes part of the learning process, rather than a shortcut.

    It has been revealed that for Rodgers, what matters is having control over how she uses the technology. As a self-employed developer, she can use AI to automate the parts of a project she finds tedious, while keeping the more interesting problem-solving for herself.

    Sources indicate that she believes there's something vital about working through a difficult problem rather than immediately outsourcing it to technology. Friction and discomfort, she stated, are vital parts of the human experience.

    In a recent development, "As humans, we need to feel accomplished in something and part of accomplishment requires challenge," she noted. "Unless we are able to work that through in so many different aspects of life, then you never get the full force of the good feeling on the other side.".

    #73677. Latest Update: Europe's cyber weak spot is the everyday businesses nobody thought to protect

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1011 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Europe's cyber weak spot is the everyday businesses nobody thought to protect

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1011 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that cyberattacks on refrigerators in French supermarkets in October spurred Swedish chain Coop to act.
    • Attackers hit refrigeration systems in seven of its stores in early November.
    • Mundane but essential equipment, used by everyday businesses, has become a favorite target of cyber saboteurs in recent weeks.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that cyberattacks on refrigerators in French supermarkets in October spurred Swedish chain Coop to act. But it wasn't fast enough.

    Attackers hit refrigeration systems in seven of its stores in early November. The affected stores had been scheduled for security upgrades just two days later, a organization spokesperson told CNBC.

    Mundane but essential equipment, used by everyday businesses, has become a favorite target of cyber saboteurs in recent weeks.

    Experts are warning that a combination of known vulnerabilities, basic security failures and ambiguity over whether suppliers or their clients are responsible are making things worse, as AI makes cyber threats faster and more sophisticated.

    Guy Segal, CEO of cybersecurity firm Sygnia, told CNBC that his tech giant handled 285% more incidents in October than a year earlier, with demand forcing it to turn away some businesses seeking emergency assistance.

    "It's going to get worse before it's going to get better," Segal said.

    The recent cyberattacks targeted refrigeration systems across hundreds of European supermarkets, remotely altering temperature settings and forcing retailers to discard spoiled food.

    France has since accused a cyber unit with links to Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps of the attacks, an allegation Tehran denies.

    Fredrik Blix, a cybersecurity researcher at Stockholm University, told CNBC that thousands of industrial control systems remain accessible over the public internet, sometimes despite manufacturers' warnings.

    Segal noted that basic cyber protection measures such as multi-factor authentication and basic network segmentation are more important than ever.

    He said risks to major civic infrastructure like the electrical grid were front of mind and so "usually pretty well protected.".

    "There are always those civil supply chain components that are way, way less protected. Could be supermarkets, could be gas stations, could be… the screens on the Tube," Segal mentioned, referring to London's underground rail system.

    The supermarket attacks revealed "this is the fresh normal, and definitely it's a wake-up call for every organization out there," Segal added.

    Recent findings suggest that segal mentioned that inexpensive AI tools mean technical expertise and resources are no longer needed to launch attacks. He described one recent incident in which clients suffered breaches within six hours of a vulnerability becoming known, as perpetrators used AI to act faster — a process that might have taken weeks a year earlier.

    Segal, whose firm helps companies respond to breaches and strengthen their defenses, warned that businesses without prearranged incident-response support could struggle to secure emergency assistance, as overwhelmed cybersecurity firms prioritize existing clients.

    Industry observers note that in one case, he said, Sygnia had to turn down a company because no response teams were available. Segal added that the company in question had already been turned down by ten other providers.

    Jacob Silverman, CEO of risk advisory firm Kroll, told CNBC earlier this month that the manufacturer was operating at full capacity in its incident-response business amid what he described as "the most rapid uptick in threat activity that we've ever seen.".

    Segal argued that retailers should treat cybersecurity risks with the same seriousness as fire safety and food hygiene, including when outsourcing maintenance.

    In a recent development, when Ahold Delhaize stores in Belgium and Luxembourg were attacked on Nov. 2, it exposed how different independent store operators had responded to the warnings following the earlier attacks in France.

    Retailers had been warned about the vulnerabilities following earlier attacks in France, and those that implemented the recommended protections were spared, CEO Frans Muller told investors in an earnings call earlier this month, but smaller operators with fewer technical resources had struggled to make the necessary changes.

    Coop, whose stores are owned by regional consumer cooperatives or operated by franchises, told CNBC that public attention on the recent attacks was the main driver of security improvements. It remarked the vulnerability at the affected stores had since been addressed.

    The financial consequences of cyberattacks can be substantial. Ahold Delhaize told investors in November that a separate October cyberattack on its online operations and supply chain would reduce fourth-quarter sales by 200 million euros ($219 million).

    Danish shipping giant Maersk, which suffered an estimated $250 million to $300 million in losses from the 2017 NotPetya cyberattack, has spent nearly a decade strengthening its defenses.

    CEO Vincent Clerc told CNBC earlier this month that the experience had prompted significant investment in security capabilities, but warned that AI was enabling attackers to become more effective.

    "Everybody is in a race" to boost defenses, he said.

    Research by cybersecurity firm Censys found that the number of internet-exposed refrigeration controllers made by Danfoss and Copeland exposed to cyber hacking fell 53% globally between Oct. 9 and Nov. 5.

    However, more than 3,100 remained exposed, and Censys said it could not determine whether the decline reflected permanent security improvements or equipment simply being taken offline.

    A Copeland spokesperson confirmed that some of its refrigeration systems were affected by the vulnerability and said it had contacted customers to reinforce cybersecurity guidance, including keeping devices off the public internet and updating software.

    Danfoss didn't respond to CNBC requests for comment.

    In the U.K., a covert cybersecurity operation has been underway to protect tens of thousands of refrigeration systems at supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants and other businesses, the BBC reported on Friday. After researchers discovered a major vulnerability in late October, cybersecurity specialists, IT teams and the U.K.'s National Cyber Security Centre worked to alert dozens of companies and secure their systems before hackers could exploit the flaw.

    The EU's Cyber Resilience Act will also impose stricter security requirements on manufacturers of connected products from December 2027.

    But the legislation does not require all existing equipment to be made compliant with the fresh standards.

    Blix told CNBC on Nov. 6 that European authorities should take a more proactive approach to reducing vulnerabilities by identifying exposed industrial control systems and contacting their operators before attacks occur.

    "What worries me is that we don't really do anything," he noted, adding that "we are shuffling a lot of papers" and "doing a lot of risk assessments" but failing to take meaningful action.

    Cardinals QB Carson Beck ruled out, 40-year-old Josh Johnson to start vs. Chiefs

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (382 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Yahoo

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Arizona Cardinals are turning to their fourth quarterback of the season.
    • On Saturday, the team ruled out quarterback Carson Beck for Sunday's game against the Kansas City Chiefs.
    • Beck, who is a rookie, was thrust into the role of starter after Gardner Minshew went on injured reserve with a torn UCL.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Arizona Cardinals are turning to their fourth quarterback of the season.

    On Saturday, the team ruled out quarterback Carson Beck for Sunday's game against the Kansas City Chiefs. Beck has been dealing with back spasms and did not practice on Friday. Head coach Mike LaFleur remarked that the team was preparing for Josh Johnson to be the team's starter for Week 11.

    Beck, who is a rookie, was thrust into the role of starter after Gardner Minshew went on injured reserve with a torn UCL. The Cardinals' original starter, Jacoby Brissett, was traded to the Baltimore Ravens after being benched for Minshew mid-game the week before.

    Beck had been listed as questionable on Friday's injury report.

    LaFleur noted that this is an issue that Beck has dealt with before, but wasn't able to provide a clear timeline for a return.

    In a recent development, in the meantime, the 40-year-old Johnson, who was signed off the Cincinnati Bengals' practice squad after the Minshew injury, will step up for Sunday's matchup against the Chiefs. At 40 years, 191 days, Johnson will be the second-oldest non-specialist to appear in a game for the Cardinals behind only Jim Thorpe (41 years, 185 days old), according to the team.

    The itinerant backup quarterback also has some history with LaFleur: Johnson and LaFleur's careers overlapped in 2021, when both were with the Fresh York Jets (LaFleur was an offensive coordinator at the time). LaFleur had high praise for Johnson, noting some of the reasons he's been able to keep his career going this long.

    "If it is Josh, I've called plays for him before, and had a really great experience calling plays for him," LaFleur stated. "He is incredible in the quarterback room, he's incredible for the starters. He's incredible for young quarterbacks, in terms of the way he sees the game, his energy, his positivity, how he keeps it real. He's mature. And he can still sling it. … If that's the route that ends up happening, let's go.".

    Arizona is the 15th NFL franchise that Johnson has been a part of in his career, as the veteran quarterback has bounced between half of the teams in the league. Across 16 seasons, he has only started 11 games in his NFL career.

    So much for buying the dip.As the S&P 500 entered correction territory and the Nasdaq-100 flirted with bear-market territory, down 19% from highs as of midday Friday, the single biggest options trade of the day was a near $100-million bet that the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) has a long way more to fall.Around 12:30 E.T., someone spent $93 million buying 20,000 380-strike puts expiring Sep. 17, 2027, according to trading data reviewed by SpotGamma and Volland, options-analytics platforms that both show the trade as a likely opening position, with volume exceeding existing open interest in the contract. The trade bets that the index will fall below $380, a nearly 8% decline from its current level. The SMH is off 40% from its recent all-time highs.

    "That trade stands out massive-time," wrote Jason DeLorenzo, founder and owner of Volland. "It is either a hedge or speculative, but either way it isn't a vote of confidence."The puts were bought for $46.50 a piece, an arguably expensive choice for a downside bet with volatility in the ETF trading at 70.

    Industry observers note that "You're paying a metric ton of Vega for that thing," added SpotGamma's Brent Kochuba, referring to the contract's sensitivity to changes in volatility of the underlying chip ETF. "Maybe they were a forced buyer, or maybe they're actually selling this, which can still be the case even though the price shows it happening closer to the ask.".

    The semiconductor index headed for a 9% drop this week alone.

    #73670. Tech Report: What's ahead for AI financing after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang departs

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (740 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: What's ahead for AI financing after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang departs

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (740 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure hasn't produced a broad shock to the credit market, but it is putting the company's role as a financier of artificial intelligence infrastructure under scrutiny.
    • In a recent development, huang, who stepped down Thursday amid an espionage and adultery scandal, built Nvidia into an AI powerhouse in the 33 years since he co-founded the tech giant.
    • Nvidia not only supplies its graphics processing units to hyperscalers and tech giants, it also provides financing to other companies to help the industry expand.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure hasn't produced a broad shock to the credit market, but it is putting the company's role as a financier of artificial intelligence infrastructure under scrutiny.

    In a recent development, huang, who stepped down Thursday amid an espionage and adultery scandal, built Nvidia into an AI powerhouse in the 33 years since he co-founded the tech giant. Chief financial officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO as the company searches for a permanent chief executive.

    Nvidia not only supplies its graphics processing units to hyperscalers and tech giants, it also provides financing to other companies to help the industry expand. That could all change.

    "Although we expect the tech giant to fulfill all of its previously announced commitments, we believe that going forward, it may be more difficult for the company to negotiate upcoming multi-party investments among ecosystem partners at the same scale it has done up to this point," Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider remarked in a note Thursday.

    The news of Huang's resignation comes after investors were already concerned about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure.

    According to recent reports, tech bond yields have risen and spreads have widened on credit default swaps, most notably in lower-rated names. Credit default swaps are contracts in which investors pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. Wider spreads indicate investors view the bonds as riskier.

    On Friday, the yield on Nvidia's 4.5% bond due in 2031 sat at 5.717%, nearly 5% higher week to date. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

    Industry observers note that tech stocks slumped Friday with the Nasdaq 100 closing down 1.2% as markets continued to digest the Nvidia news. Yields on hyperscaler bonds ticked slightly higher on Friday, signaling the broader concern about AI debt lingers.

    According to recent reports, it's the smaller AI companies that could ultimately see an impact if Nvidia makes any changes to its AI financing. The manufacturer had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, or backstops, for neoclouds, according to its last quarterly financial filing in July.

    Neoclouds CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN are all in Nvidia's portfolio. Their shares were down sharply Thursday.

    CoreWeave, which has become the poster child for AI debt fears, saw its bond yields retreat after its quarterly earnings on Tuesday eased investor concerns. The yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 was 14.79% on Friday after climbing to 16.7% last week. The spread on its five-year CDS also dropped more than 17% week to date, although it remained above 1,000 — which is generally considered a sign of distress.

    It remains unclear how Nvidia's support for those companies may change, said CreditSights analyst Andy Li.

    "We don't know what the ultimate strategy for Nvidia is going to be coming out the other side," he mentioned.

    "However, I think directionally, just given the fact that Jensen was so crucial in selling the Nvidia story and being a very aggressive deal maker, it's likely that a lot of this creative deal-making and circular financing and equity and credit support is going to moderate," he added.

    CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC Wednesday, before Huang's departure, that Nvidia "is not one person.".

    "There are thousands of people over there that interface with thousands of people at my firm every day. They integrate on the technology. They integrate on the physical infrastructure. They integrate on the networking," he remarked in an interview with "Squawk on the Street." "They have been a great partner for us for years. They will continue to be a great partner for us.".

    Bob Lang, founder and chief strategist at Explosive Options, doesn't see any significant changes in terms of Nvidia's relevance or its ability to finance for now. As CFO, Kress was involved in the financing deals, and the search for a permanent CEO is going to take some time, he noted.

    The real glitch is just how much money the company will want to lend for AI financing, rather than, say using its hundreds of billions in free cash flow for other purposes, like share buybacks, capex, or acquisitions.

    "Significant companies like Nvidia and Meta, they're holding all the cards," he remarked. "When they decide that the game is over, that's it — it's going to be curtains for some of these smaller companies.".

    — CNBC'S Kif Leswing and Isabel O'Brien contributed reporting.
